name: Transparency International (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: changes in policy, law and practice from global rules (the UN anti-corruption convention's resolution on political finance) to EU law and national laws in the chapters' countries across more than 100 countries (97% of the result at the defaults), with the advice centres in 53 countries and legal cases mostly in Europe; no country split is published, so the result is spread by world population, most of it in low- and middle-income countries (a judgment).
summary: Transparency International's Secretariat in Berlin, with offices in Brussels and Washington, campaigns for global, EU and national anti-corruption rules, brings legal cases and funds and supports more than 100 national chapters, whose legal advice centres help people who meet corruption; it spent EUR 28.0 million ($31.6 million) in 2025. Its year is counted as its share of the 60-plus changes in policy, law and practice the movement contributed to, each removing a judged small share of what corruption costs the people it governs (corruption's cost taken as about the 2% of income paid in bribes), building up over about four years and lasting the years a won reform counts unless repealed; smaller branches count the 14,000 people the advice centres supported and the 62 legal submissions (public money recovered, and deterrence). With the next dollar at about half the average, that comes to about 0.07 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, about the site's global-health median. The result is mostly uncertainty, its own ranges spanning millions-fold: the biggest are judgments with no study behind them, the share of corruption's cost a change removes and the people an average change governs. All three branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: Everything Transparency International's Secretariat in Berlin and its offices in Brussels and Washington spent in 2025, from the audited consolidated statements, in dollars at the year's average rate. Grants to national chapters count as the work they fund; administration and the essential functions (fundraising, evaluation, the CEO's office) are spread over the programmes.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The year's output as the annual report counts it: changes in policy, law and practice the movement contributed to, and the people they govern; people supported by the chapters' legal advice centres; legal submissions against corruption.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What each output is worth in income: a change removes a share of what corruption costs the people it governs, building up over a few years and lasting the years a win counts unless repealed; a person redressed gets back a share of a year's consumption; a successful case returns public money, spread over the people whose budget it is. All on the log-consumption scale.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's own discounts for trust in the evidence, the share that would have happened anyway, the Secretariat's share of the resources behind the result, enforcement and missing data, and its side effects; the canonical rows are their averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

Changes in policy, law and institutional practice the work contributed to, 2025

source.title: Transparency International, Annual Report 2025 (17 July 2026)
source.quote: 60+ Changes in policy, law and institutional practice that Transparency International contributed to.

rows.explainer: Transparency International's own count for 2025, at least 60: 63 (60 to 70). They range from global and EU rules (the UN anti-corruption convention's resolution on political finance, the EU's ban on golden passports, two articles of the EU anti-corruption directive) to national strategies and laws (the Integrity Pact in Spain's anti-corruption strategy, Switzerland's beneficial-ownership act) and agencies' practice. The count is the organisation's, not an independent one.

rows.label: People governed by the average change
rows.explainer: Each change covers the people of the place whose rules change. The annual report's eight highlights include global and EU rules (about 450 million people in the EU) beside national ones in countries of 5 to 50 million people, and many changes are an agency's or a city's practice, covering fewer. The average, which large rules pull up: 30 million (5 to 150 million). Soft or voluntary rules count their full population here and their weak force in implementation_adj.

rows.label: People supported by the chapters' Advocacy and Legal Advice Centres, 2025

source.title: Transparency International, Annual Report 2025 (17 July 2026)
source.quote: Last year, ALACs in 53 countries supported over 14,000 people.

rows.explainer: Free, confidential advice to people who met or witnessed corruption, given by national chapters in 53 countries; the Secretariat funds part of it through partner support and runs the shared data system and guides.

rows.label: Anti-corruption legal submissions, 2025

source.title: Transparency International, Annual Report 2025 (17 July 2026)
source.quote: Transparency International worked with 11 national chapters and four external partners on strategic legal casework and 62 anti-corruption submissions.

rows.explainer: Complaints, evidence to prosecutors, amicus briefs and civil-party filings brought with 11 chapters and four partners, mostly in Europe (the Azerbaijani Laundromat conviction in Munich, the Steward Health Care arbitration in Malta, a case in France about a banana producer in Cameroon).

rows.label: People per year the changes won and the casework reach
rows.explainer: Everyone governed by the year's changes plus the people the legal advice centres supported; the legal submissions' gain is public money, spread over whole populations, so it adds no count here.

rows.label: People released, cleared or kept out of detention by casework in the year
rows.explainer: 0: the work frees no one from detention; the legal advice centres' casework is counted as income in its own branch.

rows.label: Bribes paid each year, as a share of income
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): about 2% of the world's income. A measure of what is at stake, not the loss: the next row turns it into income lost.

rows.label: Income lost to corruption per dollar of bribes
rows.explainer: A bribe is mostly a transfer; the loss is what corruption distorts: contracts to the wrong firm, roads that cost more and last less, investment and taxes forgone. The IMF's note that the bribes are about 2% of world income says the wider economic and social costs are larger still; the public-investment gap alone (about 27% of public investment's value lost in emerging markets, @democracy.public_investment_efficiency_gap_emerging, on public investment of a few percent of GDP) is of the same order as the bribes. Judged 1 (0.3 to 3): corruption's income cost about 2% of income.

source.title: IMF, Corruption: Costs and Mitigating Strategies (staff discussion note, May 2016) and its summary
source.note: Anchor, not the figure: the note estimates bribery at about 2% of global GDP and says the broader costs are larger.

rows.label: Share of corruption's cost a change removes where it is applied

source.title: Olken (2007), Monitoring Corruption: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Indonesia, Journal of Political Economy 115(2): 200-249 (abstract)
source.quote: increasing government audits from 4 percent of projects to 100 percent reduced missing expenditures ... by eight percentage points

rows.explainer: The largest measured effects are within one sector: in Olken's trial in Indonesia, certain audits cut the money missing from village road projects by 8 percentage points, about a third of what went missing (about 24%). A national law, rule or agency practice touches a few sectors among many, and most changes are smaller steps: disclosure rules, a register, a strategy, reporting duties. Judged 0.3% of a country's whole income cost of corruption per change (0.03% to 2%), applied as written; how far it is applied is implementation_adj.

rows.label: Income gained per person governed per year (log consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + corruption's income cost × the share a change removes): the gain in log consumption for each person governed, the same scale wherever they live.

rows.label: Chance the change happens
rows.explainer: 1: the changes are already in; Transparency International's share of them is in the attribution rows, and the chance they'd have come anyway in the years a win counts.

rows.label: Years a won change counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9): the years a won reform is brought forward.

rows.label: Years from the change until it starts to bite
rows.explainer: Laws and rules usually apply within a year of adoption; EU directives take two years to enter national law and the UN resolution needs national laws: 1 year (0.5 to 3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
Yearly chance a won change is undone
rows.explainer: The shared hazard for won reforms of how governments work (facts/democracy.json): anti-corruption rules are also attacked and rolled back (in Slovakia a 2025 law weakened the whistleblower protection authority before the constitutional court suspended it, annual report p. 44; the EU Court of Justice's 2022 ruling ended public access to beneficial-ownership registers).

rows.label: Discount rate plus the repeal hazard
Years until a change's full effect
rows.explainer: A change takes effect as institutions use it: a register is filled and searched, prosecutors take cases, firms adapt; the gain builds up evenly over these years. Audits in Olken's trial worked within a project cycle; registers and disclosure rules take years. 4 years (1 to 10), shorter than democracy's 25-year build-up (@democracy.democratization_years_to_effect), which is a whole regime's.

rows.label: Discounted years of the full gain per change
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + pol_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + pol_rate) ^ (0 - pol_ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + pol_rate) * ln(1 + pol_rate) * pol_ramp_years) * pol_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The family's shifted ramp (families/rights-advocacy.md): a gain building up over pol_ramp_years, brought forward by the years a win counts, at the discount rate plus the repeal hazard, after the wait.

rows.label: Income gained from the year's changes, in units of value (before adjustments)
Share of people supported whose problem is put right

source.title: Transparency International Bosnia and Herzegovina, ALAC Annual Report 2021
source.quote: In 2021, ALAC handled a total of 265 new cases, of which 26 were initiated by ALAC itself and the remaining 239 were cases where ALAC acted on the basis of reports/complaints received from citizens.

rows.explainer: Most people supported get advice by phone or in person; a smaller number become cases the centre acts on, and some of those end with the bribe refused, the service given, the land or money returned. The Bosnian centre took on 265 cases against 1,629 calls in 2021 (cases about 14% of contacts); no published figure gives the share resolved. 10% (3% to 30%).

rows.label: What a person gets back when the problem is put right, as a share of a year's consumption
rows.explainer: A bribe not paid, a pension, school place or health service obtained, a plot of land or wages recovered (the annual report's example is a Malagasy family's land): from a small sum to more than a year's consumption for land. Counted once, present value: 30% of a year's consumption (5% to 150%).

rows.label: Income gained per person redressed (log consumption, once)
Years from advice to redress
rows.explainer: Administrative complaints settle in months; court cases take years: half a year (0 to 2).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
Income gained by people redressed, in units of value (before adjustments)
Share of submissions that end in a sanction, recovery or money saved
rows.explainer: Submissions include evidence to prosecutors, complaints and amicus briefs; prosecutions and arbitrations take years and many end without a result. The annual report names a conviction (Munich) and a EUR 148 million claim rejected (Malta) among 62. 15% (5% to 35%).

rows.label: Public money recovered or saved per successful submission

source.title: Transparency International, Annual Report 2025 (17 July 2026)
source.quote: The International Chamber of Commerce Arbitral Tribunal later rejected a €148 million claim by Steward Health Care

rows.explainer: One case in 2025 saved Malta EUR 148 million (about $167 million) in an arbitration where Transparency International's amicus brief was one voice; most successes are convictions, fines or confiscations far smaller, and some recover nothing beyond the sanction. Typical, the Malta case being the far tail: $2 million ($0.2 to $30 million). Deterrence is a side effect, below.

rows.label: Yearly consumption per person where the money returns
rows.explainer: The casework is mostly in Europe (Germany, Malta, France) with some in middle-income countries through chapters; household consumption per person in the EU is about $20,000 to $30,000, in middle-income countries a few thousand. Judged $12,000 ($4,000 to $30,000). Money returned to a public budget is spread over everyone there, so the gain in log consumption, summed over them, is the money ÷ this figure.

rows.label: Years from submission to recovery
rows.explainer: Prosecutions and arbitrations take years: the Laundromat conviction came about a decade after the scheme was exposed; most cases are shorter. 2 years (1 to 5).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
Public money recovered or saved, in units of value (before adjustments)
Wellbeing gained per person affected per year (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: 0: gains are counted as income; wellbeing beyond income is a side-effect share.

rows.label: Health gained per person affected per year (DALYs)
rows.explainer: 0: the work's health gains (services that reach people, less money stolen from health budgets) are inside the income gain.

rows.label: Income gained per person affected (log consumption; average over the policy and advice-centre branches)
rows.formula: (pol_changes * pol_people_per_change * pol_ln_gain + alac_people * alac_redressed_share * alac_ln_gain) / people_affected_per_year
rows.explainer: For reading only: each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Chance of success (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_p_success + alac_raw * alac_redressed_share + enf_raw * enf_success_share) / raw_total
rows.explainer: For reading only: the policy changes are in (1), the casework branches' success shares are their own.

rows.label: Years until effect (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_years_until_effect + alac_raw * alac_years_until_effect + enf_raw * enf_years_until_effect) / raw_total
rows.explainer: For reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.label: Discount for the wait (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_wait_discount + alac_raw * alac_wait_discount + enf_raw * enf_wait_discount) / raw_total
rows.explainer: For reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.label: Discounted years (policy branch; the casework is one-off)
rows.explainer: The policy branch's discounted years; the casework branches count a one-off gain.

rows.label: Years of detention avoided per person released
rows.explainer: 0: no one is released (released_people).

rows.label: Wellbeing gained per year out of detention
rows.explainer: 0: no one is released (released_people).

rows.label: Wellbeing per person released
Trust that a change on paper lowers corruption's cost (policy branch)
rows.explainer: Few anti-corruption rules have been tested: top-down audits have (Olken 2007), community monitoring did little in the same trial, and the evidence on registers, disclosure and agencies is mostly before-after or cross-country. Half (0.25 to 0.85), lower than for an intervention with trials behind it.

rows.label: Share that wouldn't have happened anyway (policy branch)
rows.explainer: 1: whether a change would have come anyway is the years a win counts (Convention 5), not a second discount.

rows.label: The Secretariat's share of the movement's resources behind the changes
rows.explainer: The count is the movement's: national chapters, with their own budgets and donors, led many of the national changes (Spain's chapter on the Integrity Pact), while the Secretariat led the global and EU ones and funds chapters' work through its EUR 13.6 million of partner support. The chapters' combined spending isn't published; the Secretariat's EUR 28.0 million against chapters' budgets, many of which are under a million euros, puts its share at about 40% (20% to 70%).

rows.label: Transparency International's share of all groups' resources behind the changes
rows.explainer: Other NGOs (Global Witness, Open Ownership, ONE, the FACT coalition, OCCRP's reporting), donors and international bodies pushed the same changes, and governments' own reformers did most of the work. Credit by share of the resources behind the wins (Convention 2): about 30% (10% to 60%), as one of the largest specialised groups in most of the coalitions named.

rows.label: The Secretariat's credit for the changes
Share of a change applied as written (policy branch)
rows.explainer: Anti-corruption rules are often weakly enforced, and some changes are voluntary or soft law (the UN climate talks' disclosure rule, the UN resolution, which needs national laws). 40% (15% to 70%).

rows.label: Missing-data discount (policy branch)
rows.explainer: Thin: the changes are the organisation's own count and the effect per change is judged, not measured (Convention 12).

rows.label: All adjustments (policy branch)
Fair treatment by the state beyond income, as a share of the policy branch
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json) for what better government is worth beyond income, from Helliwell and Huang (2008), who find the quality of government, of which corruption is a main part, linked to life satisfaction beyond its link through income.

rows.label: Backlash against the work, as a share of the policy branch
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): campaigns invite counter-measures. Chapters face foreign-agent laws and closures (Russia declared Transparency International undesirable in 2023; the Secretariat helped Venezuelan colleagues relocate in 2025, annual report p. 6).

rows.label: Side effects, as a share of the policy branch
Trust in the redress figures (advice-centre branch)
rows.explainer: The share redressed and what it is worth are judged from the centres' own case reports, which no independent study checks: 0.75 (0.5 to 1).

rows.label: Share of the redress that wouldn't have happened without the centre
rows.explainer: Some people would have got redress through an ombudsman, a lawyer or persistence; the centres serve people who usually can't pay for one and say most would have given up (the annual report quotes a farmer: without the centre 'we would have given up'). 60% (30% to 90%).

rows.label: The Secretariat's share of the resources behind the centres
rows.explainer: The centres are run by national chapters with their own grants; the Secretariat funds some through partner support (the civic-space programme's EUR 1.6 million of partner support), runs the shared case system and writes the guides. 30% (10% to 60%).

rows.label: Share of reported support delivered as counted
rows.explainer: 1: the people counted are those the centres supported; how many got redress is alac_redressed_share.

rows.label: Missing-data discount (advice-centre branch)
rows.explainer: Thin: the count is the organisation's, and the share redressed and its worth are judged (Convention 12).

rows.label: All adjustments (advice-centre branch)
Retaliation against people who report, as a share of the advice-centre branch
rows.explainer: Some who report corruption face reprisals (job loss, threats); the centres advise confidentially and refer whistleblowers to protection, which limits it: -3% (-15% to 0).

rows.label: Side effects, as a share of the advice-centre branch
Trust in the recovery figures (legal-submission branch)
rows.explainer: 1: the sums and the success share are judged directly with wide ranges; a second discount would count the same doubt twice (Convention 5).

rows.label: Share of the result that wouldn't have happened without the submission
rows.explainer: Prosecutors and governments act on their own in many cases; Transparency International's evidence or brief was decisive in some (the Malta tribunal admitted its brief; the Laundromat case followed years of its pressure). 50% (20% to 80%).

rows.label: The Secretariat's share of the resources behind the successful cases
rows.explainer: Prosecutors, courts and governments carry the cost of a case; of the civil-society side, the chapters and four partners share the work. 20% (5% to 50%) of what the submissions add.

rows.label: Share of sums awarded actually recovered
rows.explainer: 1: enf_money_per_success is money recovered or saved, not money awarded.

rows.label: Missing-data discount (legal-submission branch)
rows.explainer: Thin: the outcomes of the submissions aren't published; success share and sums are judged (Convention 12).

rows.label: All adjustments (legal-submission branch)
Deterrence of other corruption, as a share of the legal-submission branch
rows.explainer: A conviction or a lost claim deters others beyond the money at stake; Olken's audits worked through the threat of sanction. No study measures how much one case deters: as much again as the money (20% to 400%).

rows.label: Side effects, as a share of the legal-submission branch
Trust in the effect (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_evidence_adj + alac_raw * alac_evidence_adj + enf_raw * enf_evidence_adj) / raw_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share applied as counted (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_implementation_adj + alac_raw * alac_implementation_adj + enf_raw * enf_implementation_adj) / raw_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.label: Missing-data discount (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_missing_data_adj + alac_raw * alac_missing_data_adj + enf_raw * enf_missing_data_adj) / raw_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_total_adj + alac_raw * alac_total_adj + enf_raw * enf_total_adj) / raw_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_attribution_share + alac_raw * alac_attribution_share + enf_raw * enf_attribution_share) / raw_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit used (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Side effects (weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pol_raw * pol_total_adj * pol_unmodelled_benefits_adj + alac_raw * alac_total_adj * alac_unmodelled_benefits_adj + enf_raw * enf_total_adj * enf_unmodelled_benefits_adj) / (pol_raw * pol_total_adj + alac_raw * alac_total_adj + enf_raw * enf_total_adj)
rows.explainer: For reading only: every branch adds its own side effects.
